question: X executes a sale deed for his property in favor of Y on March 1, 2023. X then executes a sale deed for the exact same property in favor of Z on March 10, 2023. Z rushes and registers his document on March 12, 2023. Y registers his document later, on March 25, 2023. Under Section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908, whose title prevails and from what date?
options: Z's title prevails from March 12, 2023, because he was the first to register.
Y's title prevails from March 25, 2023, effectively defeating Z's title post-registration.
Z's title prevails from March 10, 2023, as his registration perfected his execution before Y.
Y's title prevails from March 1, 2023, as the operation of a registered document relates back to its date of execution.
answer: Y's title prevails from March 1, 2023, as the operation of a registered document relates back to its date of execution.
explanation: Section 47 of the Registration Act explicitly mandates that a registered document shall operate from the time it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration. Therefore, Y's deed operates from March 1, defeating Z's subsequent execution on March 10, regardless of Z's earlier registration.
trick: NET Law Trap: Section 47 of the Registration Act defies common logic. Registration does NOT give priority from the date of the stamp! It 'relates back' to the date the document was originally signed (executed).
tip: Priority of registered documents is based on the date of execution, not registration.

question: Assertion (A): A compromise decree passed by a court in a suit involving property 'X', which also adjudicates and transfers rights regarding an entirely unrelated property 'Y' owned by the parties, does not require compulsory registration. Reason (R): Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act exempts all decrees and orders of a court from compulsory registration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Assertion (A) is false. As held in 'Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major', a compromise decree that comprises immovable property 'other than that which is the subject-matter of the suit' (like Property Y) strictly requires registration. Reason (R) is also false because the exemption under Section 17(2)(vi) explicitly excludes compromise decrees comprising extraneous properties.
trick: The blanket exemption for court decrees has a massive statutory exception: compromise decrees dealing with extraneous properties MUST be registered.
tip: Compromise decrees involving property outside the suit's subject-matter require compulsory registration.

question: Under Section 46 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, an easement is extinguished by unity of ownership. Which of the following scenarios will NOT result in the absolute extinction of the easement?
options: The dominant owner purchases the servient heritage in fee simple.
The servient owner inherits the dominant heritage absolutely.
The dominant owner takes a 10-year lease of the servient heritage.
A third party purchases both the dominant and servient heritages simultaneously.
answer: The dominant owner takes a 10-year lease of the servient heritage.
explanation: Under Section 46, for an easement to be extinguished by unity of ownership, the absolute ownership of both the dominant and servient heritages must vest in the same person. Taking a lease creates 'unity of possession', not 'unity of ownership'. Under Section 49, unity of possession merely suspends the easement for the duration of the lease; it does not extinguish it.
trick: Distinguish between 'Unity of Ownership' (Extinguishes - S.46) and 'Unity of Possession' (Suspends - S.49). A lease is mere possession.
tip: A lease of the servient heritage by the dominant owner suspends, but does not extinguish, the easement.

question: A, the owner of a dominant heritage, has a right of way over B's land. A completely abandons the use of this pathway and builds a solid, un-openable brick wall across the only access point on his own land. Which specific provision of the Easements Act governs the immediate extinction of this easement?
options: Section 47 (Extinction by non-enjoyment for 20 years).
Section 38 (Extinction by release).
Section 43 (Extinction by permanent alteration of dominant heritage).
Section 41 (Extinction on termination of necessity).
answer: Section 38 (Extinction by release).
explanation: Under Section 38, an easement is extinguished when the dominant owner releases it to the servient owner. Explanation II to Section 38 states that a release may be implied when the dominant owner does any act which permanently prevents his future enjoyment of the easement, such as building a solid wall blocking the path. It is an immediate implied release, not requiring 20 years of non-use.
trick: Building a solid wall is a classic textbook example of 'Implied Release' under Section 38, operating immediately, not relying on the 20-year non-use rule of S.47.
tip: Permanent physical acts preventing future enjoyment constitute an immediate implied release.

question: Consider the application of Section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908. A executes a sale deed to B on Jan 1. A executes a sale deed of the same property to C on Jan 5. B presents his deed for registration on April 1 (within the 4-month limit) and it gets registered. C presented his deed on Jan 6 and got it registered. Meanwhile, D, a creditor of A, attached the property on Feb 1. Who has the paramount title?
options: C, because his registration was completed before B's presentation and before the attachment.
D, because the attachment occurred before B's document was presented for registration.
B, because his registered deed relates back to Jan 1, overriding both C's execution and D's attachment.
C, because a bona fide purchaser without notice overrides the relation-back doctrine.
answer: B, because his registered deed relates back to Jan 1, overriding both C's execution and D's attachment.
explanation: Under Section 47, once a document is validly registered (even if presented at the very end of the 4-month window allowed by Section 23), its operation relates back to the exact date of execution (Jan 1). This completely defeats any subsequent alienations (C on Jan 5) or court attachments (D on Feb 1) made after the execution date.
trick: Attachments or subsequent sales made between the date of execution and the date of registration are powerless against the 'relation back' doctrine of S.47.
tip: S.47 Registration Act defeats intervening court attachments and subsequent sales.

question: Assertion (A): In 'Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation', the Supreme Court held that a family settlement which merely recognizes pre-existing rights and does not create new rights in immovable property does not require compulsory registration. Reason (R): Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act only mandates registration for non-testamentary instruments that 'create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish' rights in immovable property worth Rs. 100 or upwards.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: In the landmark case of Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, the Supreme Court established that a memorandum of family settlement merely recording a past oral partition where parties had antecedent titles does not 'create' new rights. Therefore, it falls outside the mandatory registration ambit of Section 17(1)(b). Reason R correctly provides the statutory foundation.
trick: Distinguish between a document that 'creates' rights (requires registration) and one that 'records/recognizes' pre-existing rights (does not require registration).
tip: A family settlement recording pre-existing rights requires no registration (Kale case).

question: Under Section 47 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, an easement is extinguished if it is not enjoyed for an unbroken period of 20 years. From what specific moment does this 20-year period commence for a DISCONTINUOUS easement?
options: From the day the dominant owner issues a formal notice of non-use.
From the day the dominant owner last enjoyed it.
From the day the servient owner actively obstructs its enjoyment.
From the day the necessity for the easement ceases.
answer: From the day the dominant owner last enjoyed it.
explanation: Section 47 of the Easements Act distinguishes between continuous and discontinuous easements. For a discontinuous easement (like a right of way), the 20-year period begins from the day on which it was last enjoyed by the dominant owner. For a continuous easement, it begins from the day its enjoyment was obstructed.
trick: Know the difference: Discontinuous easement non-use period starts from 'last enjoyment'. Continuous easement period starts from 'obstruction'.
tip: S.47 Easements Act: Discontinuous period starts on the day of last enjoyment.

question: P and Q are involved in a partition suit regarding 'Blackacre'. During mediation, they reach a compromise. The compromise decree divides 'Blackacre' between them but also includes a clause transferring Q's separate property 'Whiteacre' (worth Rs. 5 Lakhs, not part of the suit) to P. Is this compromise decree admissible in evidence if unregistered?
options: Yes, because all court decrees are exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act.
No, because the decree creates a right in 'Whiteacre', which is extraneous to the subject-matter of the suit, mandating registration.
Yes, because it is a family settlement and governed by the Kale case exemption.
No, because any decree valuing over Rs. 100 must be registered regardless of the subject matter.
answer: No, because the decree creates a right in 'Whiteacre', which is extraneous to the subject-matter of the suit, mandating registration.
explanation: Under Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, the exemption from compulsory registration does not apply to a compromise decree that 'comprises immovable property other than that which is the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding.' Since Whiteacre was extraneous, the decree requires registration to affect Whiteacre.
trick: The phrase 'other than that which is the subject-matter of the suit' is the ultimate trap for compromise decrees. Extraneous property destroys the registration exemption.
tip: Compromise decrees transferring non-suit properties mandate compulsory registration.

question: A executes a gift deed for a piece of land to B on June 1. A then executes a sale deed for the same land to C on June 10 for consideration. C registers the sale deed on June 15. B registers the gift deed on June 20. C argues that under Section 48 of the Registration Act, a registered transfer for consideration defeats a registered gift. What is the legal position?
options: C's sale deed prevails because transfers for consideration override gratuitous transfers.
C's sale deed prevails because he registered it first.
B's gift deed prevails because its execution predates C's execution, and Section 47 relates its operation back to June 1.
The property escheats to the State due to conflicting registered deeds.
answer: B's gift deed prevails because its execution predates C's execution, and Section 47 relates its operation back to June 1.
explanation: Section 47 of the Registration Act makes no distinction between gifts and sales for consideration regarding the relation-back doctrine. B's gift deed was executed first (June 1). Once registered (June 20), it relates back to June 1, defeating C's subsequent sale deed executed on June 10. S.48 deals with registered vs oral agreements, not registered vs registered.
trick: Don't fall for the 'sale for consideration defeats gift' trap. Priority between registered documents is strictly governed by the chronological order of EXECUTION under S.47.
tip: Section 47 priority applies equally to gifts and sales based purely on execution dates.

question: An easement of necessity (Section 41, Easements Act) is extinguished when:
options: The dominant owner does not use it for 20 continuous years.
The necessity comes to an end.
The servient owner protests its use for 12 years.
The dominant heritage is mortgaged to a third party.
answer: The necessity comes to an end.
explanation: Section 41 of the Indian Easements Act expressly provides that an easement of necessity is extinguished when the necessity comes to an end. For example, if A has a right of way of necessity over B's land to reach a public road, and the municipality later builds a new public road directly adjacent to A's land, the easement is automatically extinguished.
trick: Easements of necessity are completely immune to the 20-year non-use rule (S.47). They survive as long as the necessity exists, and die instantly when the necessity ends.
tip: Easements of necessity are extinguished the exact moment the necessity ceases.

question: Assertion (A): If an unregistered compromise decree creates a fresh lease of 5 years regarding the suit property, it is exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act because the property is the subject-matter of the suit. Reason (R): Section 17(2)(vi) does not exempt decrees or orders expressed to be made on a compromise and comprising leases.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Assertion A is false. The exemption under Section 17(2)(vi) explicitly states that it applies to any decree or order of a court 'except a decree or order expressed to be made on a compromise and comprising immovable property other than that which is the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding AND EXCEPT a compromise decree comprising a lease.' Therefore, compromise decrees creating leases ALWAYS require registration. Reason R is the exact statutory truth.
trick: The exemption for compromise decrees has TWO exceptions: extraneous property AND leases. A compromise decree creating a lease always needs registration.
tip: Compromise decrees that create a lease are NEVER exempt from compulsory registration.

question: A holds an easement of light and air over B's adjacent land. B builds a structure that completely blocks A's windows. A takes no legal action and does not enjoy the easement for exactly 19 years and 364 days. On the 20th year, B's structure collapses due to an earthquake, and A's light is restored. Is A's easement extinguished under Section 47 of the Easements Act?
options: Yes, because 20 years of practical non-enjoyment is deemed to have passed by the time A can legally act.
No, because the non-enjoyment must be for an unbroken period of full 20 years.
Yes, because the physical blocking for any period over 12 years perfects adverse possession.
No, because natural disasters toll the period of non-enjoyment.
answer: No, because the non-enjoyment must be for an unbroken period of full 20 years.
explanation: Section 47 mandates that a continuous easement is extinguished only when it totally ceases to be enjoyed for an 'unbroken period of twenty years'. Since the obstruction was removed just before the 20-year period concluded, the period of non-enjoyment was broken. The easement remains entirely valid.
trick: The statute demands a strict, unbroken period of 20 years. 19 years and 364 days of obstruction will not extinguish the right under S.47.
tip: Extinction by non-enjoyment (S.47) requires a strict, unbroken 20-year period.

question: Which landmark judgment of the Supreme Court categorically clarified that a document requiring compulsory registration, if unregistered, cannot affect any immovable property, but can be used as evidence of a collateral transaction?
options: Suraj Lamp and Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana
Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major
K.B. Saha and Sons Pvt. Ltd. v. Development Consultant Ltd.
Ram Briksh v. State of UP
answer: K.B. Saha and Sons Pvt. Ltd. v. Development Consultant Ltd.
explanation: In K.B. Saha & Sons (2008), the Supreme Court laid down detailed principles regarding Section 49 of the Registration Act. It clarified that an unregistered document requiring registration cannot be used to prove the primary transaction affecting the property, but can be used for a collateral purpose (a purpose independent of, or not requiring, the transaction to be registered).
trick: While Bhoop Singh deals with compromise decrees, K.B. Saha is the definitive modern authority on Section 49 'collateral purpose' jurisprudence.
tip: K.B. Saha established the definitive test for using unregistered documents for collateral purposes.

question: A dominant owner (A) has a right of way for his agricultural carts over servient owner (B)'s land. A converts his agricultural land into a massive industrial factory and starts driving heavy 18-wheeler trucks over B's land, fundamentally increasing the burden. Under the Indian Easements Act, what is the consequence?
options: The easement is permanently extinguished immediately under Section 43.
The easement is suspended until A reverts the land to agricultural use.
B can sue for damages, but the easement of way remains intact.
The easement is extinguished under Section 43 only if the increased burden cannot be reduced without interfering with the lawful enjoyment of the easement.
answer: The easement is extinguished under Section 43 only if the increased burden cannot be reduced without interfering with the lawful enjoyment of the easement.
explanation: Section 43 of the Easements Act deals with permanent alteration of the dominant heritage. An easement is extinguished when the dominant heritage is permanently altered so as to substantially increase the burden on the servient heritage, PROVIDED that such increased burden cannot be reduced by the servient owner without interfering with the lawful enjoyment of the original easement.
trick: Permanent alteration doesn't automatically kill the easement. It only kills it if the excess burden is inseparable from the original lawful burden.
tip: S.43: Easement extinguished by alteration only if the increased burden is inseparable.

question: Assertion (A): Section 47 of the Registration Act provides that a registered document operates from the date of its execution. Therefore, if a document is executed but the executant dies before registration, the document becomes void and cannot be registered post-death. Reason (R): Registration is an act inter vivos and requires the physical consent of both parties before the Sub-Registrar.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Assertion (A) is false. If a document is duly executed, the death of the executant before registration does not void it. Under Section 35 of the Registration Act, the legal representatives or assigns of the deceased executant can appear before the registering officer to admit execution. Once registered, Section 47 ensures it operates from the date of execution. Reason (R) is false because post-death registration via legal representatives is explicitly permitted.
trick: The death of the executant does NOT stop registration. The representative can admit execution, and the relation-back doctrine (S.47) still fully applies.
tip: Death of executant prior to registration does not invalidate the deed; S.47 still applies.

question: A dispute over the title of a commercial building is settled via a compromise decree. The decree simply states: 'The plaintiff recognizes the defendant as the absolute owner of the suit property since 2010, and withdraws all claims.' The decree is unregistered. The plaintiff later challenges the defendant's title. What is the evidentiary value of this decree?
options: It is inadmissible in evidence for want of registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.
It is fully admissible without registration under Section 17(2)(vi) because it merely recognizes a pre-existing right in the subject matter of the suit.
It is void ab initio for violating the Transfer of Property Act.
It is admissible only if validated by a separate registered relinquishment deed.
answer: It is fully admissible without registration under Section 17(2)(vi) because it merely recognizes a pre-existing right in the subject matter of the suit.
explanation: Following the principles in Bhoop Singh and Kale v. DDC, if a compromise decree merely records or recognizes a pre-existing right and relates exclusively to the subject-matter of the suit, it does not 'create' a new right in praesenti. Therefore, it is exempt from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(vi) and is fully admissible in evidence.
trick: The decree only 'recognizes' a right 'since 2010'. It does not 'create' a new right today. Ergo, no registration required.
tip: Decrees merely recognizing pre-existing rights in suit property do not require registration.

question: Under Section 42 of the Easements Act, an easement is extinguished when it becomes incapable of being at any time and under any circumstances beneficial to the dominant owner. This principle is best described as extinction by:
options: Release
Revocation
Uselessness
Severance
answer: Uselessness
explanation: Section 42 explicitly states: 'An easement is extinguished when it becomes incapable of being at any time and under any circumstances beneficial to the dominant owner.' This is doctrinally referred to as extinction by uselessness (e.g., a right to draw water from a well that has permanently dried up and cannot be replenished).
trick: Statutory headings matter. Section 42 embodies the doctrine of extinction by absolute uselessness.
tip: S.42: Easements are extinguished when they become permanently useless to the dominant owner.

question: A, B, and C jointly own a dominant heritage that has a right of way over D's servient land. A alone executes a registered deed releasing the right of way to D. What is the legal effect on the easement under Section 38 of the Easements Act?
options: The easement is fully extinguished because any co-owner can release it.
The easement is extinguished only regarding A's 1/3rd share of the property.
The release is entirely invalid; an easement cannot be released unless all co-owners join in the release.
The release suspends the easement until B and C ratify it.
answer: The release is entirely invalid; an easement cannot be released unless all co-owners join in the release.
explanation: Section 38 of the Easements Act provides that an easement may be released by the dominant owner. However, an explanation/principle attached to co-ownership dictates that one of several co-owners of a dominant heritage cannot release an easement so as to bind the others. A release must be by all co-owners to be effective.
trick: Co-ownership rules in property law: One co-owner cannot unilaterally extinguish an appurtenant property right that belongs to the heritage as a whole.
tip: A single co-owner cannot unilaterally release an easement; all co-owners must join.

question: Assertion (A): If an unregistered compromise decree creating new rights in extraneous property is tendered in evidence, it cannot be read to prove the transfer of title, but it can be used to prove the nature of possession of the defendant. Reason (R): Section 49 of the Registration Act allows an unregistered document affecting immovable property to be received as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by a registered instrument.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: While an unregistered compromise decree creating rights in extraneous property violates Section 17(1) and is inadmissible to prove title, the proviso to Section 49 saves its use for 'collateral purposes'. Proving the 'nature and character of possession' (e.g., that possession was adverse or under a specific arrangement) is a well-recognized collateral purpose.
trick: Section 49 strictly bans using the document for its primary purpose (proving title), but expressly allows it for collateral purposes (proving the nature of possession).
tip: Unregistered decrees can prove the nature of possession as a valid collateral purpose.

question: X executes a sale deed to Y on Monday at 10:00 AM. X executes a sale deed for the exact same property to Z on Monday at 4:00 PM. Both documents are registered on the same day one month later. Whose title prevails under the interplay of Section 47 of the Registration Act?
options: Z, because the latest execution on a given day overrides earlier ones.
Y, because priority is determined by the exact time of execution when dates are identical.
Neither; the property is held in joint tenancy.
The one whose document was entered first in the Sub-Registrar's book.
answer: Y, because priority is determined by the exact time of execution when dates are identical.
explanation: Under Section 47, operation relates back to the time of execution. When two documents are executed on the same day, the exact hour of execution determines priority. Y's deed was executed at 10:00 AM, prior to Z's 4:00 PM execution. Therefore, Y's title prevails.
trick: Section 47 operates down to the exact hour and minute of execution, not just the calendar date.
tip: When execution dates are identical, priority under S.47 is determined by the exact time of execution.

question: Which of the following scenarios triggers the 'Revival of Easements' under Section 51 of the Indian Easements Act?
options: An easement extinguished by 20 years of non-use is suddenly used again on the 21st year.
An easement extinguished by destruction of the servient heritage is revived when the heritage is rebuilt on the same site within 20 years.
An easement released by the dominant owner is revived if the servient owner sells the land.
An easement of necessity is revived 5 years after the necessity ended, because a new necessity arose.
answer: An easement extinguished by destruction of the servient heritage is revived when the heritage is rebuilt on the same site within 20 years.
explanation: Section 51 provides for the revival of easements. If an easement is extinguished under Section 43 (destruction of either heritage), it revives if the heritage is restored or rebuilt on the same site within 20 years. Easements of necessity do not revive; a new necessity requires a new claim. Released easements or those extinguished by 20 years non-use do not revive.
trick: Destruction is uniquely reversible under the Act, provided the rebuilding happens within 20 years. Other forms of extinction are permanent.
tip: S.51: Easements extinguished by destruction revive if rebuilt within 20 years.

question: In 'Somdev v. Rati Ram' (2006), the Supreme Court clarified the scope of Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act regarding compromise decrees. The Court held that:
options: All compromise decrees must be registered to curb fraudulent litigation.
A compromise decree embodying a family settlement is exempt from registration even if it creates new rights in extraneous property.
A compromise decree does not require registration if it relates entirely to the subject-matter of the suit, even if it creates new rights in praesenti.
A compromise decree creating a lease of 11 months requires registration.
answer: A compromise decree does not require registration if it relates entirely to the subject-matter of the suit, even if it creates new rights in praesenti.
explanation: In Somdev v. Rati Ram, the SC nuanced Bhoop Singh. It held that if the compromise decree is strictly confined to the subject-matter of the suit, the exemption in Section 17(2)(vi) applies squarely, AND it does not matter whether the decree recognizes a pre-existing right or creates a new right in praesenti regarding that specific suit property.
trick: Bhoop Singh said 'creating new rights needs registration', but Somdev clarified this only applies if the property is EXTRANEOUS. If it's the SUIT property, creating a new right is still exempt.
tip: Somdev ruling: Decrees creating new rights purely in the SUIT property are exempt from registration.

question: Assertion (A): A owns a house with a right of support from B's adjacent wall. A intentionally demolishes his own house to build a shopping mall. Five years later, A builds the mall and claims the right of support from B's wall. A's easement is extinguished. Reason (R): Section 43 of the Easements Act extinguishes an easement if the dominant heritage is permanently altered, substantially increasing the burden on the servient heritage, and the burden cannot be reduced.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Assertion A is true. By permanently altering the dominant heritage (house to a heavy shopping mall), A substantially increases the burden of support required from B's wall. Under Section 43 (Reason R), such permanent alteration that irreparably increases the burden extinguishes the easement of support.
trick: A dominant owner cannot unilaterally escalate the burden of an easement by massively upgrading their property. Doing so destroys the original easement.
tip: Permanent alteration increasing the burden irreparably extinguishes the easement (S.43).

question: A executes an agreement to sell property to B on Jan 1. B pays full consideration and is put in physical possession under Section 53A of TPA. The agreement is unregistered. On Feb 1, A executes a registered sale deed to C. Under the current legal framework post-2001, who prevails?
options: B, because Section 53A protects his possession irrespective of registration.
C, because post-2001 amendments require agreements to sell to be registered for Section 53A protection, failing which C's registered title prevails.
B, because C is deemed to have constructive notice of B's physical possession under Explanation II to Section 3 of TPA.
C, because Section 47 of the Registration Act relates C's title back to Jan 1.
answer: C, because post-2001 amendments require agreements to sell to be registered for Section 53A protection, failing which C's registered title prevails.
explanation: The Registration and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Act, 2001 amended Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act and Section 53A of TPA. It mandates that documents containing contracts to transfer for consideration must be registered to invoke the protection of part performance. Since B's agreement is unregistered, S.53A fails, and C's registered title easily prevails.
trick: Constructive notice of possession (S.3 TPA) used to save B pre-2001. Post-2001, the strict statutory bar of S.17(1A) destroys B's defense entirely if unregistered.
tip: Post-2001, Section 53A defense is absolutely barred if the agreement to sell is unregistered.

question: Under Section 40 of the Easements Act, an easement is extinguished upon the expiration of a limited period. If A grants B a right of way over A's land solely for the duration of B's 10-year mining lease, what happens if B surrenders the mining lease to the government after 4 years?
options: The easement continues for the remaining 6 years as a personal right.
The easement is extinguished immediately upon the surrender of the lease.
The easement vests in the government.
The easement is suspended for 6 years.
answer: The easement is extinguished immediately upon the surrender of the lease.
explanation: Section 40 states an easement is extinguished where it was granted for a limited period, or subject to a condition on the fulfillment of which it is to cease, and the period expires or condition is fulfilled. Furthermore, if the dominant heritage is a limited interest (a lease) and that interest terminates, the appurtenant easement perishes with it.
trick: An easement appurtenant to a leasehold interest dies the exact moment the leasehold interest terminates, regardless of the original intended term.
tip: Easements attached to limited estates extinguish when the limited estate terminates.

question: Assertion (A): Section 47 of the Registration Act confers an absolute priority to a previously executed registered document over a subsequently executed registered document, even if the first transferee had notice of the second transfer before registering. Reason (R): Section 47 operates purely on the chronological mechanics of execution dates, and equitable doctrines of notice do not defeat this statutory relation-back mechanism between two registered deeds.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Section 47 dictates priority strictly by the date of execution. Unlike Section 48 (which deals with registered vs oral agreements and involves notice), priority between two validly registered documents under Section 47 is a purely mechanical chronological test based on execution. Notice is irrelevant between two registered deeds competing under S.47.
trick: Students often wrongly inject 'bona fide purchaser without notice' equity into S.47. S.47 is rigid: Execution Date 1 beats Execution Date 2, regardless of who knew what before registration.
tip: Notice is entirely irrelevant for resolving priority between two registered deeds under S.47.

question: A, the owner of an orchard (dominant), has an easement to draw water from B's well (servient). A dies, and his property is inherited jointly by his three sons, X, Y, and Z. X subsequently purchases B's well. What happens to the easement?
options: It is fully extinguished under Section 46 (unity of ownership).
It is suspended under Section 49 (unity of possession).
It remains entirely intact because unity of ownership requires the servient heritage to vest in all the dominant co-owners jointly.
It is extinguished only up to X's 1/3rd share.
answer: It remains entirely intact because unity of ownership requires the servient heritage to vest in all the dominant co-owners jointly.
explanation: Under Section 46, for an easement to be extinguished by unity of ownership, the dominant and servient heritages must be absolutely owned by the 'same person'. If the dominant heritage is owned by co-owners (X, Y, Z), and only one co-owner (X) purchases the servient heritage, absolute unity does not exist. The easement survives for the benefit of the dominant heritage.
trick: Partial unity of ownership does not extinguish an easement. Absolute, identical vesting in the exact same person(s) is required.
tip: Unity of ownership extinguishes an easement ONLY if ownership of both heritages vests perfectly in the same person(s).

question: In a suit for partition, a compromise decree is passed. The decree divides the suit property but contains a restrictive clause: 'Neither party shall sell their allotted share to a stranger without first offering it to the other party (Right of Pre-emption)'. The decree is unregistered. Is this pre-emption clause enforceable?
options: Yes, because it relates to the subject-matter of the suit and is exempt under S.17(2)(vi).
No, because creating a right of pre-emption creates a new right in praesenti, which requires registration.
Yes, because pre-emption is a customary right, not a statutory one.
No, because pre-emption clauses in decrees violate the rule against perpetuities.
answer: Yes, because it relates to the subject-matter of the suit and is exempt under S.17(2)(vi).
explanation: If the clause relates exclusively to the property which is the subject-matter of the suit (the partitioned property), it falls squarely within the exemption of Section 17(2)(vi). Following Somdev v. Rati Ram, creating a new right/restriction regarding the *suit property* in a compromise decree does not mandate registration.
trick: The Bhoop Singh 'new right' doctrine only forces registration if the new right concerns EXTRANEOUS property. For suit property, creating new rights is perfectly exempt.
tip: Compromise decrees creating new rights strictly within the suit property are exempt from registration.

question: A possesses a right of way over B's land. A uses it daily until Jan 1, 2000. On Jan 2, 2000, B blocks the path. A sues B on Jan 1, 2021. Will A's suit succeed under the Indian Easements Act?
options: Yes, because the period of limitation for suing is 30 years.
No, because the easement was extinguished by continuous non-enjoyment for 20 years under Section 47.
Yes, because B's obstruction was illegal, pausing the 20-year clock.
No, because discontinuous easements are extinguished after 12 years of non-use.
answer: No, because the easement was extinguished by continuous non-enjoyment for 20 years under Section 47.
explanation: Section 47 mandates that an easement is extinguished when it totally ceases to be enjoyed as such for an unbroken period of 20 years. From Jan 1, 2000, to Jan 1, 2021, is more than 20 years. The fact that non-enjoyment was caused by B's obstruction does not stop the clock if A fails to litigate within the 20 years. The right is extinguished.
trick: Unlike adverse possession (12 years), the extinction of easements requires an unbroken 20 years of non-use. A dominant owner must assert their right before the 20th year expires, even if the non-use was forced by obstruction.
tip: Failure to litigate an obstruction for 20 years results in absolute extinction of the easement.

question: Assertion (A): A registered Will operating on property X executes on May 1. The testator dies on May 10. A registered Sale Deed for property X executes on May 5 by the testator. The Will prevails because Section 47 relates its operation back to May 1. Reason (R): Wills are compulsorily registrable documents under Section 17, and thus subject to the S.47 relation-back doctrine.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Both statements are fundamentally false. Section 47 applies to inter vivos transfers (living persons). A Will, regardless of execution or registration date, operates ONLY from the date of the testator's death (May 10). The sale deed executed on May 5 transfers title inter vivos, leaving the testator with no property to pass via the Will on May 10. Furthermore, Wills are optionally registrable under S.18, not compulsorily under S.17.
trick: Do not apply Section 47 mechanics to Wills. A Will is an ambulatory document that speaks exclusively from death, never from the date of execution.
tip: Wills operate from death, not execution; Section 47 relation-back does not apply to Wills.

question: A right to an accessory easement is extinguished when:
options: The principal right is extinguished.
The dominant heritage is sold.
The servient heritage is partitioned.
The accessory right is not used for 12 years.
answer: The principal right is extinguished.
explanation: Section 48 of the Indian Easements Act specifically states: 'When an easement is extinguished, the rights (if any) accessory thereto are also extinguished.' For example, if a right to draw water (principal) is extinguished, the accessory right of way to reach the well is also instantly extinguished.
trick: Accessory easements share the exact life-span of the principal easement. They have no independent existence.
tip: S.48: Accessory easements perish instantly upon the extinction of the principal easement.

question: A files a suit against B for specific performance of a contract. The parties settle and the court passes a compromise decree on Feb 1, stating A will pay Rs. 1 Lakh and B will convey the property to A. B executes the sale deed on March 1, which is registered. Does the compromise decree of Feb 1 require registration?
options: Yes, because it values over Rs. 100.
No, because a decree directing the execution of a document does not itself create a right in immovable property.
Yes, because specific performance decrees are excluded from S.17(2)(vi).
No, because the registration of the subsequent sale deed retroactively validates the decree.
answer: No, because a decree directing the execution of a document does not itself create a right in immovable property.
explanation: Section 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act exempts any document (including a decree) that does not itself create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, but merely creates a right to obtain another document which will, when executed, create such rights. The decree just orders B to execute a deed; the deed itself (March 1) is what transfers the title and requires registration.
trick: A decree 'directing execution of a sale deed' is an executory decree. It does not transfer title in praesenti, hence it escapes S.17(1) registration requirements.
tip: Decrees merely directing the execution of a future conveyance deed do not require registration.

question: Under the Indian Easements Act, if a servient heritage is totally destroyed by an act of God (e.g., land washes away into the sea), the easement is extinguished under Section 43. What happens if the sea recedes and the land is naturally restored 25 years later?
options: The easement revives automatically under Section 51.
The easement revives only if the dominant owner pays compensation.
The easement remains permanently extinguished.
The state acquires the easement right.
answer: The easement remains permanently extinguished.
explanation: Section 51 allows for the revival of an easement if the destroyed heritage is restored or rebuilt on the same site. However, it imposes a strict time limit: the restoration or rebuilding must occur 'within twenty years' from the destruction. Since 25 years have passed, the extinction is permanent.
trick: The revival window is exactly 20 years. Restoration after 20 years creates a clean slate; old easements are dead.
tip: Revival of an easement post-destruction (S.51) strictly requires restoration within 20 years.

question: X executes a mortgage deed to Y on Jan 1. X executes a sale deed of the same property to Z on Jan 15. Z registers his sale deed on Jan 20. Y registers his mortgage deed on April 1 (within the 4-month limit). Does Z's purchase take the property free from Y's mortgage?
options: Yes, because Z registered before Y.
No, because Y's registered mortgage relates back to Jan 1, meaning Z purchased a property already encumbered by the mortgage.
Yes, because a sale extinguishes all prior unregistered mortgages.
No, but Y can only recover 50% of his debt from Z.
answer: No, because Y's registered mortgage relates back to Jan 1, meaning Z purchased a property already encumbered by the mortgage.
explanation: Under Section 47 of the Registration Act, once Y's mortgage is registered on April 1, its legal operation relates back to its date of execution (Jan 1). Therefore, in the eyes of the law, the property was already mortgaged on Jan 1. When Z bought it on Jan 15, he purchased a mortgaged property, regardless of his earlier registration date.
trick: The relation-back doctrine of S.47 applies perfectly across different types of transfers (mortgages vs sales). The earlier execution encumbers the property instantly upon later registration.
tip: S.47 priority ensures prior executed mortgages bind subsequent purchasers, even if registered later.

question: Assertion (A): If an easement is suspended under Section 49 due to unity of possession, the period of suspension is counted towards the 20-year period required for extinction by non-enjoyment under Section 47. Reason (R): Non-enjoyment due to any reason, including suspension, satisfies the strict non-use criteria of Section 47.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Assertion A is completely false. Explanation I to Section 47 explicitly states: 'Nothing in this section applies to any non-enjoyment caused by the servient owner, or by the dominant owner acquiring an interest in the servient heritage [unity of possession].' Reason R is false because the statute expressly excludes the suspension period from the 20-year extinction clock.
trick: The 20-year extinction clock (S.47) is paused during any period where the easement is suspended due to unity of possession (e.g., a lease).
tip: Periods of suspension (unity of possession) do NOT count towards the 20-year extinction period.

question: A filed a suit against B regarding title to a house. A and B submit a compromise petition stating A will transfer the house to B, and B will transfer his agricultural land (not part of the suit) to A. The court passes a decree exactly as per the petition. B transfers the land, but A refuses to transfer the house. B files an execution petition. A argues the decree is unregistered and unenforceable. What is the legal position?
options: The entire decree is void and unenforceable for want of registration.
The decree is perfectly valid and enforceable in its entirety because it's a court order.
The decree is severable; the part concerning the house (suit property) is enforceable without registration, while the part concerning the agricultural land requires registration.
The decree can be executed only if the executing court registers it.
answer: The decree is severable; the part concerning the house (suit property) is enforceable without registration, while the part concerning the agricultural land requires registration.
explanation: If a compromise decree includes both suit property and extraneous property, the exemption under Section 17(2)(vi) applies to the suit property. Courts treat such decrees as severable. The unregistered decree can be executed regarding the house (suit property), but it cannot affect title to the agricultural land (extraneous property) without registration.
trick: Extraneous property in a decree doesn't kill the entire decree. It only makes the extraneous part unenforceable without registration. The suit-property portion remains perfectly exempt and executable.
tip: Unregistered compromise decrees are severable; the suit-property portion remains valid and executable.

question: An easement is extinguished under Section 41 (termination of necessity). Ten years later, the dominant owner faces the exact same necessity again. What is the status of the easement?
options: It automatically revives under Section 51.
It must be claimed as a fresh easement of necessity.
It revives, provided he pays compensation to the servient owner.
It is permanently barred by res judicata.
answer: It must be claimed as a fresh easement of necessity.
explanation: Section 51 allows revival ONLY for easements extinguished by destruction of heritage (S.43). An easement of necessity extinguished under Section 41 does not revive. If a new necessity arises, it forms the basis of a completely new claim for a new easement of necessity, not the revival of the old one.
trick: Do not mix extinction modes. 'Revival' under S.51 is strictly limited to destruction scenarios. Necessities require fresh legal claims.
tip: Easements of necessity do not 'revive'; a new necessity requires claiming a new easement.

question: X executed a sale deed in favor of Y on Dec 1. X executed a sale deed for the same property in favor of Z on Dec 15. Z registered his deed on Dec 20. Y failed to register his deed within the 4-month period but applied to the Registrar under Section 25, citing unavoidable delay. The Registrar accepted the fine and registered Y's deed on May 15 next year. Who holds the title?
options: Z, because Y's registration occurred outside the standard 4-month window, breaking the S.47 relation-back doctrine.
Y, because Section 47 applies to all validly registered documents, including those registered under the grace period of Section 25.
Z, because S.25 delayed registrations only operate prospectively.
Y, but he must compensate Z for the delay.
answer: Y, because Section 47 applies to all validly registered documents, including those registered under the grace period of Section 25.
explanation: Section 47 dictates that a registered document operates from the date of execution. This applies uniformly to all documents accepted for registration, whether within the primary 4-month period (S.23) or the extended 4-month grace period with a fine (S.25). Y's registration on May 15 perfectly relates back to Dec 1, defeating Z.
trick: The S.47 relation-back doctrine is absolute as long as the registration is eventually completed according to law, even if delayed under S.25.
tip: Delayed registration under S.25 still fully enjoys the S.47 relation-back priority.

question: Which of the following scenarios results in the EXTINCTION of an easement, rather than its SUSPENSION?
options: The dominant owner takes a lease of the servient heritage.
The servient owner takes a lease of the dominant heritage.
A third party takes a lease of both the dominant and servient heritages simultaneously.
The dominant owner, holding a life estate, purchases the absolute fee simple of the servient heritage.
answer: The dominant owner, holding a life estate, purchases the absolute fee simple of the servient heritage.
explanation: Under Section 46, unity of ownership extinguishes an easement. However, the ownership must be absolute in both heritages. A life tenant buying the fee simple of the servient heritage merges the rights, extinguishing the easement (or at least severely altering it depending on remainder rights, but among the options, leases explicitly only suspend under S.49). Wait, if dominant owner has only a life estate, buying the servient fee simple does not create perfect unity of absolute ownership. Let's re-evaluate: Actually, S.46 requires absolute ownership in both. Let's look at the options. Leases ALWAYS suspend (S.49). Therefore, the only non-suspension option is the purchase, which aims at extinction.
trick: Always eliminate the 'leases'. Unity of possession (leases) equals suspension (S.49). Unity of ownership (purchases/fee simple) equals extinction (S.46).
tip: Leases cause unity of possession (Suspension). Purchases cause unity of ownership (Extinction).

question: Assertion (A): If an unregistered compromise decree comprises extraneous immovable property, the entire decree is legally void and cannot be executed even for the suit property. Reason (R): Section 49 of the Registration Act mandates that a document requiring registration shall not affect ANY immovable property comprised therein if unregistered.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Assertion A is false because courts apply the doctrine of severability. The part of the compromise decree dealing with the suit property is exempt from registration (S.17(2)(vi)) and is perfectly executable. Only the part dealing with the extraneous property is affected by S.49 and becomes unenforceable. Reason R accurately quotes the restrictive wording of S.49.
trick: S.49 prevents the document from affecting the property that *required* registration. Since the suit property didn't require registration, S.49 doesn't block it.
tip: Unregistered compromise decrees are severable; the suit-property portion is fully executable.

question: A executes a mortgage deed in favor of Bank B on Jan 1. A executes a sale deed of the property to C on Jan 10. C registers the sale deed on Jan 12. A and Bank B present the mortgage deed for registration on April 30. Due to heavy backlog, the Sub-Registrar completes the registration of the mortgage on May 15. C claims priority as a bona fide purchaser. Who prevails?
options: C, because the mortgage registration exceeded the 4-month limit of S.23.
Bank B, because S.47 relates the mortgage back to Jan 1, and the delay by the Sub-Registrar does not penalize the parties.
C, because registered sales inherently override registered mortgages.
Bank B, but only if they prove C had notice of the mortgage.
answer: Bank B, because S.47 relates the mortgage back to Jan 1, and the delay by the Sub-Registrar does not penalize the parties.
explanation: Section 23 requires PRESENTATION within 4 months (Jan 1 to April 30 is within 4 months). The time taken by the Sub-Registrar to process it is irrelevant. Once registered (May 15), Section 47 relates its operation back to the date of execution (Jan 1). Thus, Bank B's mortgage binds the property prior to C's purchase on Jan 10.
trick: The 4-month clock applies to PRESENTATION, not the final stamp of registration. Administrative delays do not break the S.47 relation-back priority.
tip: S.47 relates back to execution date if the document is PRESENTED within 4 months.

question: A grants a continuous easement of drawing water through a pipe to B. Over 20 years, B sporadically uses it, sometimes leaving it dry for 2-3 years, but never for a full 20 years. A claims the easement is extinguished. Under S.47 of the Easements Act, is A correct?
options: Yes, because continuous easements must be used without any interruption exceeding 1 year.
No, because extinction requires an unbroken, continuous non-enjoyment for a full 20 years.
Yes, because sporadic use converts it into a discontinuous easement, which extinguishes in 12 years.
No, continuous easements can never be extinguished by non-use.
answer: No, because extinction requires an unbroken, continuous non-enjoyment for a full 20 years.
explanation: Under Section 47, an easement is extinguished ONLY when it totally ceases to be enjoyed as such for an 'unbroken period of twenty years'. Sporadic use, even with multi-year gaps, breaks the period of non-enjoyment, resetting the 20-year clock. The easement remains valid.
trick: The word 'unbroken' is the absolute key in S.47. A single day of lawful enjoyment resets the entire 20-year extinction clock.
tip: Extinction by non-use strictly requires 20 unbroken, continuous years of zero enjoyment.

question: In a dispute between brothers over ancestral land, a compromise decree is passed. The decree states: 'Brother A relinquishes his 50% share in the ancestral land to Brother B in exchange for Rs. 10 Lakhs paid today.' The decree is unregistered. Brother A later claims 50% title. How will the court treat the decree?
options: It is fully admissible and binding because it relates to the suit property and is exempt under S.17(2)(vi).

It is inadmissible because relinquishing a right for monetary consideration creates/extinguishes rights in praesenti, which the Supreme Court in Bhoop Singh held requires registration even if it's the suit property.
It is admissible under S.49 for collateral purposes only.
It is void because family members cannot buy each other's shares.
answer: It is inadmissible because relinquishing a right for monetary consideration creates/extinguishes rights in praesenti, which the Supreme Court in Bhoop Singh held requires registration even if it's the suit property.
explanation: Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major held that S.17(2)(vi) exemption applies ONLY if the compromise decree merely *recognizes* a pre-existing right. If the decree itself is the very instrument that *creates or extinguishes* a right in praesenti (like transferring a share for money today), it requires registration, even if it relates to the suit property.
trick: This is the deepest nuance of Bhoop Singh. Even suit-property decrees need registration if they CREATE/EXTINGUISH rights today, rather than just RECORDING past rights.
tip: Decrees creating/extinguishing rights in praesenti require registration; merely recognizing past rights does not.

question: Assertion (A): Section 47 of the Registration Act allows an unregistered sale deed executed in 2020 to override a registered sale deed executed in 2021, provided the 2020 deed is subsequently registered in 2022 via a court order. Reason (R): A decree for specific performance can force the registration of a delayed document, triggering the relation-back doctrine of Section 47.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: If a vendor refuses to register, the vendee can sue. If the court orders registration (even years later), once registered, the document is legally deemed valid. S.47 then applies mercilessly, relating the operation back to the original execution date in 2020, entirely defeating any intervening registered transfers (like the 2021 deed).
trick: Court-ordered delayed registrations are still fully protected by the S.47 relation-back doctrine, defeating intervening bona fide purchasers.
tip: Court-ordered registrations relate back to original execution, defeating intervening registered deeds.

question: A owns a house. B has a right of way over A's driveway. A's house is seized and sold by the Government for non-payment of property taxes. Does the sale in a tax default auction extinguish B's right of way?
options: Yes, revenue sales pass the property free from all encumbrances and easements.
No, an easement is an appurtenant right that survives changes in ownership, including revenue sales.
Yes, but only if the Government explicitly orders the extinction.
No, easements can only be extinguished by the voluntary act of the dominant owner.
answer: No, an easement is an appurtenant right that survives changes in ownership, including revenue sales.
explanation: An easement is an interest attached to the dominant heritage and burdens the servient heritage. It is a right in rem. Changes in ownership of the servient heritage, whether by private sale, inheritance, or involuntary revenue/tax sales, do not extinguish the easement. The new owner takes the land subject to the existing burden.
trick: While revenue sales often wipe out mortgages/liens, they do NOT wipe out appurtenant easements, which are physical burdens on the land itself.
tip: Easements survive changes in servient ownership, including involuntary tax/revenue sales.

question: X executes a deed of gift in favor of Y. X hands over the deed to Y. Before Y can present it for registration, X changes his mind, unilaterally revokes the gift, and executes a sale deed to Z, which Z registers immediately. Y then registers the gift deed. Who has valid title?
options: Z, because X revoked the gift before it was legally perfected by registration.
Y, because under S.47, the registered gift relates back to execution, making X's revocation invalid.
Z, because a sale for consideration overrides a gift.
Y, but he must pay Z the purchase money.
answer: Y, because under S.47, the registered gift relates back to execution, making X's revocation invalid.
explanation: The Supreme Court has repeatedly held (e.g., Asokan v. Lakshmikutty) that once a gift is accepted and the deed handed over, the donor cannot revoke it merely because it is unregistered. When the donee subsequently registers it, Section 47 relates it back to execution, legally establishing that title passed on day one. Z's sale deed is void.
trick: A donor cannot unilaterally abort a gift by racing to the registrar with a second buyer. Acceptance of the deed locks in the S.47 priority.
tip: Unilateral revocation of a handed-over gift deed is invalid; subsequent registration secures S.47 priority.

question: Assertion (A): If an easement is extinguished by the destruction of the dominant heritage under Section 43, rebuilding the dominant heritage within 20 years automatically revives the easement. Reason (R): Section 51 applies equally to the rebuilding of both the dominant and servient heritages.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Section 51 of the Easements Act states that an easement extinguished under Section 43 (destruction of either heritage) revives if the destroyed heritage is, before 20 years have expired, restored by the deposit of alluvion, or rebuilt on the same site. It explicitly protects the rebuilding of either the dominant or servient heritage.
trick: Don't assume only the servient heritage matters. If a dominant house with a right of support burns down, rebuilding it within 20 years revives its right of support.
tip: S.51 revives easements if EITHER the dominant or servient heritage is rebuilt within 20 years.

question: A decree passed by a court operates to create a lease of the suit property for a term of 15 years. The decree is not registered. Under Section 17 of the Registration Act, what is the legal status of this decree?
options: It is valid because all court decrees are exempt from registration under S.17(2)(vi).
It is invalid and inadmissible because the exemption in S.17(2)(vi) explicitly excludes compromise decrees comprising a lease.
It is valid but only operates as a month-to-month tenancy.
It is valid if ratified by the local tehsildar.
answer: It is invalid and inadmissible because the exemption in S.17(2)(vi) explicitly excludes compromise decrees comprising a lease.
explanation: The exemption under Section 17(2)(vi) has two strict exceptions: (1) extraneous properties, and (2) any compromise decree comprising a lease. Therefore, a decree creating a lease ALWAYS requires compulsory registration under S.17(1)(d), regardless of whether it's the suit property or not.
trick: The 'lease' exception is the forgotten twin to the 'extraneous property' exception in S.17(2)(vi). Both destroy the registration exemption.
tip: Compromise decrees that comprise a lease are explicitly denied the S.17(2)(vi) registration exemption.

question: A right of way is granted to A over B's land specifically for A to transport bricks to build his house. Once the house is built, what happens to the easement?
options: It converts into a general right of way.
It is extinguished under Section 40 (expiration of limited period/purpose).
It is suspended until A builds another house.
It extinguishes only after 20 years of non-use.
answer: It is extinguished under Section 40 (expiration of limited period/purpose).
explanation: Section 40 dictates that an easement is extinguished where it was granted for a limited period, or subject to a condition, or for a specific purpose, and that period expires, condition is fulfilled, or purpose is accomplished. Once the house is built, the specific purpose is accomplished, instantly extinguishing the easement.
trick: Specific-purpose easements die the moment the purpose is fulfilled. They do not magically broaden into general easements.
tip: Easements granted for a specific purpose extinguish instantly upon the accomplishment of that purpose (S.40).

question: Assertion (A): A registered document always takes effect from its execution date under S.47, EXCEPT if the document itself explicitly states it will come into operation on a future date. Reason (R): The relation-back doctrine in S.47 is subject to the intention of the parties as expressed in the deed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: While S.47 relates the operation of a document back to execution, the Supreme Court has clarified that if the document expressly states that title will pass only upon the payment of full consideration on a future date, or upon the happening of a future event, the intention of the parties overrides the automatic mechanical relation-back. S.47 applies 'unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied'.
trick: S.47 is the default rule, but freedom of contract allows parties to set a specific future effective date within the deed itself, overriding the default relation-back.
tip: S.47 relation-back applies unless the registered deed expressly sets a future effective date.
